extracted.intended_audience: students, writers, teachers, and general readers learning about literary/rhetorical devices for creative writing and analysis
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and apply a wide range of literary, rhetorical, narrative, and sound devices to enhance creative writing, poetic composition, and persuasive prose; includes definitions, purposes, and examples for each device. Useful for writers learning techniques and students studying rhetoric/literary analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literary device (general definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any deliberate strategy of using language that a writer or speaker employs to more effectively achieve some purpose: focus audience attention, make language memorable, or evoke emotional/rational/aesthetic responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Covers narrative devices, poetic devices, argumentative/rhetorical devices, linguistic schemes/templates; many devices overlap categories. Purpose-driven: persuasion, memory, emphasis, emotional effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trope (term/usage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Originally an artistic effect realized with figurative (non-literal) language or a substitution of a word/phrase by a less literal one; more broadly, recurring or overused devices, motifs, character types, situations, or clichés.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize both narrow (figurative language) and broad (recurring conventions/clichés) senses; awareness of semantic change helps classify usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Figure of speech / rhetorical device (term distinction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Synonym for any literary device in technical usage; narrower colloquial use tends to mean tropes (figurative devices). Rhetorical device often refers to techniques of persuasive/argumentative language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish trope (deviation from literal meaning) vs scheme (variation in order/form). Consider ethos/pathos/logos when using rhetorical devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allegory
rubrics_metrics.description: Crafting a story with a second implicit meaning by endowing characters, setting, and events with symbolic significance so the whole story functions symbolically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each literal item often corresponds to an abstract idea or principle (example: Animal Farm as allegory for the Russian Revolution). Use when intending whole-work symbolism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flashback
rubrics_metrics.description: A scene or plot that occurs before events of the current narrative timeline used to explain plot elements, give background/context, or develop character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Can be a single scene or the device for an entire narrative framed as retrospective; ensure clarity of temporal shifts to avoid confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreshadowing
rubrics_metrics.description: Including clues about what is to come to build tension and audience suspense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subtle clues increase payoff; avoid heavy-handedness that telegraphs outcomes prematurely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mood and tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Mood is the narrative's emotional atmosphere (feelings intended for the audience); tone is the writer/speaker's attitude toward subject, reader, or self.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diction, syntax, imagery, and devices shape both; keep consistency appropriate to genre and effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motif
rubrics_metrics.description: Any word, phrase, image, or idea repeated throughout a work to develop theme, establish mood, act as symbolism, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use variety in repetition (related phrasings) and integrate motifs with themes to avoid trivial repetition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot device
rubrics_metrics.description: Any technique used to help move a story's plot forward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Can be functional (MacGuffin, deus ex machina); prefer devices that emerge organically from character/setting rather than feel artificial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story within a story / frame story
rubrics_metrics.description: A narrative presented by characters inside the context of a second narrative; when the inner narrative largely frames the main tale it becomes a frame story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use to provide perspective, distance, ironic contrasts, or nested meanings (example: Frankenstein uses a sea captain's frame).

rubrics_metrics.name: Alliteration
rubrics_metrics.description: Repetition of the sound of an initial consonant or consonant cluster (or initial vowels) across words or syllables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Creates musicality and emphasis; useful in poetry and memorable prose (example from Richard II). Avoid overuse that becomes sing-songy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assonance
rubrics_metrics.description: Repetition of similar vowel sounds inside neighboring words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Produces internal rhyme-like effects and musicality (example: 'rosy glowing ocean'); subtlety often preferred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consonance
rubrics_metrics.description: Repetition of consonant sounds across words, possibly anywhere in the word (not only initial).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different from alliteration by placement; can create texture and cohesion in lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cacophony and euphony
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of phonemes regarded as unpleasant/harsh (cacophony) or pleasant/musical (euphony) to shape auditory effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose phoneme clusters to match mood; cacophony for harsh/chaotic scenes, euphony for calm/beautiful passages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Onomatopoeia
rubrics_metrics.description: Wording that attempts to emulate a sound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common in comics/children's writing; can be used sparingly in prose for sensory immediacy. Beware colloquial typographic markers (all caps, exclamation marks).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhyming
rubrics_metrics.description: Repetition of identical or similar sounds at the ends of words/lines, often in poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Makes lines memorable and musical; choose rhyme schemes that support tone and avoid forced rhymes that distort meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amplification / Pleonasm
rubrics_metrics.description: Amplification repeats a word/expression while adding more detail to emphasize and expand a point; pleonasm uses more words than necessary, creating emphasis or additional meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use amplification to draw attention or elaborate; pleonasm can be stylistic but may be judged redundant if unmotivated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Antanagoge
rubrics_metrics.description: Placing a good point or benefit next to a fault/criticism to reduce the negative's impact or reinterpret it positively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful in persuasive writing to deflect criticism (example patterns: 'We may be managing poorly, but so did you at first' or 'When life gives you lemons, make lemonade').

rubrics_metrics.name: Apophasis (paralipsis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bringing up a subject by claiming it should not be brought up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Can indirectly emphasize or imply accusation; watch for irony or manipulative effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aporia
rubrics_metrics.description: A rhetorical expression of doubt (often rhetorical question); when answered by the speaker, it becomes hypophora.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to dramatize internal conflict or to introduce/highlight an issue (example: 'To be or not to be...').

rubrics_metrics.name: Diasyrmus
rubrics_metrics.description: Rejecting an argument through ridiculous comparison.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A satirical tool to diminish opposing views by comparison; risk of appearing dismissive if overused.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enthymeme
rubrics_metrics.description: A syllogism that omits a premise or the conclusion, relying on the reader to supply the missing part from context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective persuasion when audience can infer omitted element; ensure omission is inferable and not logically faulty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gish gallop
rubrics_metrics.description: Overwhelming an opponent by presenting an excessive number of arguments rapidly, prioritizing quantity over quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identified as a fallacious debate tactic; avoid if aiming for rigorous argumentation; recognize as a rhetorical anti-pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypophora
rubrics_metrics.description: Asking a question and immediately proceeding to answer it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful to introduce points and steer audience response; keep Q&A concise and rhetorically purposeful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Innuendo
rubrics_metrics.description: Indirectly implying an accusation without explicitly stating it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combines well with apophasis; can be persuasive but potentially unethical or damaging in polemic contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metanoia
rubrics_metrics.description: Recalling or rejecting a statement and then re-expressing it in a better or stronger way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often employs negation to amplify (example from Cymbeline); can intensify or correct previous phrasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procatalepsis
rubrics_metrics.description: Anticipating and answering a possible objection in advance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allows argument to continue while rebutting anticipated points; closely related to hypophora and strategic in persuasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhetorical question
rubrics_metrics.description: Raising a question to persuade or prompt reflection without expecting an answer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use to engage readers or emphasize a point; avoid excess that weakens argumentative clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four rhetorical operations (addition, omission, transposition, permutation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Classical categories: addition (repetition/expansion), omission (subtraction/abridgement), transposition (transferring), and permutation (switching/interchange/substitution).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These operations provide a systematic framework for creating variants of expressions and reworking source material; useful for adaptation and stylistic variation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Figurative language (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: Wording other than the ordinary literal way to provide heightened feeling, complex meaning, or deeper connection (includes metaphor, metonymy, synecdoche, irony, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Four master tropes: metaphor, metonymy, synecdoche, irony. Use figurative devices to add resonance; ensure clarity of intended non-literal relation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Implicit reference to something famous culturally, historically, or literarily.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conveys layered meaning efficiently (example: calling Beirut 'Paris of the Middle East'); ensure audience can recognize reference or supply contextual cues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Antanaclasis
rubrics_metrics.description: Word repeated in two different senses (a form of pun/wordplay).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Creates wit or emphasis by exploiting polysemy (example: Benjamin Franklin quote about 'hang together' vs 'hang separately').

rubrics_metrics.name: Anthimeria
rubrics_metrics.description: Transforming a word from one part of speech to another (e.g., noun used as verb).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Can refresh language and create vivid usage (example: 'Don't yes, sir me!'); risk of jarring if unintentionally obscure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apostrophizing (Apostrophe)
rubrics_metrics.description: Directly addressing someone absent, dead, or an inanimate/abstract object as if it were a person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to create immediacy or emotional intensity; common in poetry and oratory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogy (types)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparison showing how two different entities are alike, used to illustrate a larger point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful for explanation and persuasion; ensure analogy is apt and not misleading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metaphor
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparison between two unlike things without explicit markers (e.g., forms of 'to be'); consists of vehicle (literal) and tenor (implied meaning).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Can be extended across sentences; powerful for condensed meaning (example: 'That boy is a machine!').

rubrics_metrics.name: Simile
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicit comparison using words such as 'like' or 'as'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Makes comparisons transparent; use to clarify or evoke vivid imagery (example: 'humans in the valley look like ants').

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyperbole
rubrics_metrics.description: Deliberate exaggeration used for dramatic or persuasive effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heightens emotion or emphasis; avoid undermining credibility in contexts needing restraint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metonymy and Synecdoche
rubrics_metrics.description: Referring to a person/idea by a related object (metonymy) or using a part to refer to the whole or vice versa (synecdoche).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Efficiently evokes larger concepts (example: 'crown' for sovereign or monarchy); ensure the association is culturally intelligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personification
rubrics_metrics.description: Attributing human or animal traits to inanimate objects or non-human entities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Creates empathy or vividness (example: 'The moon smiled down'); be careful not to conflate literal and figurative layers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbolism
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of physical objects, people, actions, words, colors, or gestures to represent abstract meanings or ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Symbols can carry layered meanings (example: sun representing hope); integrate with theme to avoid arbitrary symbolism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of vivid details (often invoking senses) to cause the audience to visualize or imagine; sometimes called enargia.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine figures of speech to 'paint' with words; use sensory detail judiciously to maintain pacing and clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understatement / Meiosis / Litotes
rubrics_metrics.description: Presenting a diminished view of importance or magnitude; litotes uses negation (e.g., 'not rare').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Can be used for humor, tact, or irony; litotes often softens claims or creates ironic understatement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Irony (verbal, situational, dramatic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Language presenting something opposite to expectations. Verbal irony: saying the opposite of intent. Situational irony: events turn out opposite of expectation. Dramatic irony: audience knows something characters do not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple forms produce humor, eeriness, or poignancy. Use audience alignment and context carefully so irony registers as intended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scheme (linguistic schemes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Discourse-level device relying on intentional ordering or exact arrangement of words in phrases, clauses, or sentences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes repetition patterns, parallelism, and word-order manipulations; used to produce rhythm, emphasis, and balance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anadiplosis / Conduplicatio
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeating the last word(s) of one clause/sentence at or near the beginning of the next.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Creates linkage and momentum ('To die is to sleep; to sleep, perchance to dream'). Conduplicatio repeats a key word in subsequent clauses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anaphora / Epistrophe / Symploce / Epanalepsis
rubrics_metrics.description: Anaphora: repetition at the beginning of successive units. Epistrophe: repetition at the end. Symploce: combination of both with different words. Epanalepsis: repetition at beginning and end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Powerful for emphasis and rhythm; watch for overuse or heavy-handed sermonic tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epizeuxis
rubrics_metrics.description: Immediate repetition of the same word without interruption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conveys strong emotion or urgency ('O horror! Horror! Horror!'). Use sparsely for dramatic peaks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diacope
rubrics_metrics.description: Repetition of a word or phrase with an intervening word or clause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Produces emphasis with slight variation ('A horse! A horse! My kingdom for a horse!').

rubrics_metrics.name: Antithesis / Antimetabole / Chiasmus
rubrics_metrics.description: Antithesis: putting opposite ideas together using parallel structure. Antimetabole: repeating words in reversed order. Chiasmus: parallel structure with mirrored elements (not necessarily same words).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Creates contrast, balance, and memorable phrasing (example: 'Ask not what your country can do for you...').

rubrics_metrics.name: Asyndeton / Polysyndeton
rubrics_metrics.description: Asyndeton: omission of expected conjunctions. Polysyndeton: use of more conjunctions than needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Asyndeton speeds rhythm and creates punch; polysyndeton slows cadence and can create accumulation or solemnity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Auxesis / Catacosmesis
rubrics_metrics.description: Auxesis: arranging a list from least to most significant (creates climax). Catacosmesis: opposite order (creates anticlimax).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use ordering to build or deflate expectations; effective in speeches and comedic lists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypallage
rubrics_metrics.description: Transferring an epithet from its conventional referent to a second referent that the audience links with the first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Creates unexpected associations ('the sleepy countryside' implying sleepy people); subtlety matters for clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyperbaton
rubrics_metrics.description: Detaching or unusually rearranging words from ordinary order; more generally any figure that transposes natural word order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Can create emphasis or poetic diction; avoid obstructing comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oxymoron
rubrics_metrics.description: A two-word paradox through deliberate use of antonyms to create an internal contradiction with rhetorical effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Condenses complexity or irony ('light and heavy'); useful for poignant contrasts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Zeugma
rubrics_metrics.description: Linking two or more words/phrases that occupy the same position in a sentence to another word/phrase, often producing a double meaning or clever effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Can be clever or comic ('He caught the train and a cold'); ensure the grammatical link is clear to avoid confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction
rubrics_metrics.description: A writer's deliberate choice of specific words, communicating denotation and connotation, and shaping tone and narrator attitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Word choice reveals voice, registers, and subtext (e.g., 'stubborn' vs 'tenacious'); select words to match purpose and audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Syntax
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentence construction choices: length, active/passive voice, simple/compound/complex forms, inversion, appositives, verbal phrases, subordinate clauses, parallelism, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use sentence structure as a tool for suspense, emphasis, pacing, and voice (example from Elie Wiesel). Maintain readability aligned to effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verb choices (tense/aspect/mood)
rubrics_metrics.description: Selection and modification of verbs across tense (past/present/future), aspect (simple/perfect/progressive), and mood (indicative/imperative/interrogative/conditional/subjunctive), which convey time and attitude toward events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verb forms shape temporal perspective and narrative stance; consistent, purposeful use supports clarity and intended reading experience.
